summary: Rolling Hills sits on the Palos Verdes Peninsula, and its most striking feature is also its strictest rule: the entire city is a gated equestrian community where every residential lot must maintain horse-keeping facilities, making it one of the only incorporated cities in Los Angeles County built entirely around private bridle trails rather than sidewalks. At just three square miles and roughly 1,670 residents, this is not a town with a commercial district — there are no restaurants, no coffee shops, no grocery stores within city limits. The terrain is exactly what the name promises: rolling coastal hills with canyon-cut lots, many offering long views toward the Pacific, and annual averages of 72°F daytime highs with over nine hours of sunshine make the landscape feel perpetually Mediterranean. A median home value around $603,000 against a median household income near $92,000 yields a price-to-income ratio of about 6.6:1 — steep but not extreme by peninsula standards, partly reflecting the unusually large lot sizes and deed-restricted land use. Commuting is car-dependent; the nearest employment centers along the South Bay corridor or downtown LA sit 15 to 30-plus miles north. Property crime registers at roughly 478 per 100K, driven almost entirely by burglary, while violent crime categories report zeros across the board. Rolling Hills is essentially a rural-feeling enclave embedded in one of the country's densest metro areas — a place defined less by what it offers than by what it deliberately excludes from its borders.
